documentation:
## Particle Fireworks

### What it does

This graph utilizes the `filter_particles` node to provide controlled spawning between particle simulation systems and produce a fireworks effect.

### Inputs and outputs

The inputs to this graph are the geometries from which the fireworks will be emitted, the outputs are the fireworks particles.

### How it works

- Rather than a classic particle spawning method which emits back into the same system, the method demonstrated in this example leverages the ability to use the particles output from one simulation, as source inputs for a subsequent one. The `filter_particles` node is placed in between two particle systems to only allow particles through if they have met some criteria according to their property data. This type of simulation spawning has the advantage of easily assigning each particle emission individual influences, materials, sourcing variations etc. It has the disadvantage of not producing cascading emissions and also not providing particle to particle collisions if the particles are not in the same simulation.

- Please note that the `simulate_particles` nodes have been nested into compounds to include terminals and material assignment, for convenience.

- This simulation consists of three particle simulation systems. The `root_particles` system generates the initial particles which leave the ground and then explode into the air. The output particles of this simulation are the input for two others, after passing through the `filter_particles`: One for creating the particle trails of the root system, and one which creates the exploding particles when the root particles die. These are the `streamer_particles` and `exploding_particles` systems respectively.

- For the streamers, we simply want the root particles to start emitting after a certain age, in this case 0.2 seconds. Thus, we plug the `particles` output of the root into the `filter_particles`, set `filter_by` to `property_values`, specify `point_age` as the property and set the threshold to 0.2. We then plug the output of the filter into the streamers system. This simply reads that any particle from the root system which is aged 0.2 seconds and above, will be allowed through the filter, and will then become a source for the streamers system. Please note that the only data we will keep from the root particles is their velocity, so that the streamers can inherit from it. The streamer particles can then be tweaked and adjusted just like any regular particle system.

- For the `exploding_particles`, we actually want emission at the time of death of the root particles. Therefore we use the `killed_particles` output port from the root system. We could additionally use the filter if we wanted particles which are dead and have also met some other criteria, but in this case all the dead particles is good enough. The killed particles are passed directly into the exploding system, where things like normal speed and speed variations along with killing masked by noise, produce the specific fireworks look and behavior. Finally, these particles are also fed into a particle trails compound.

_notes.text:
# particle color
By adding a property into the *additional_properties* port on the ***source_particles*** compound, this property will be passed as a per-particle property.  In this case, a vector field is normalized, and made positive and passed in as a particle color.  These colors are passed along to all three particle simulations.

# source settings
*age_limit* and *speed* are randomized before sourcing.

***filter_particles*** is useful for secondary emission from one particle system into another. It allows one to remove points from a point object based on collide state or a specified point property along with a threshold.

# particle streamers

These are the particles "pulled out" by the projectiles.  Their source properties of *spread* and *age_limit* are varied on input - see the two ***vary_source_properties*** compound on the input stream.

The *spread* property is varied to control how much the "tails" spread out.

The *age_limit* property is varied to make some variation in how long the particles live.

# particle trails

These are the spherical "explosions" at the end of the trail.  They have a ***kill_influence*** masked by a field.  This is done to create a unique trail configuration, and the field provides a spatial randomization - that is the values are different in different places.
